raw_case_text:
A 25-year-old male presented to the Level 1 hospital with sudden onset symptoms: pyrexia (39.2 C), headache, arthralgia, myalgia, distended abdomen, watery diarrhea four times, no nausea, and vomiting. He previously had been well, and he had never been given a typhoid vaccination before. On examination, blood pressure was 120/65 mmHg; heart rate was 72 bpm. Otherwise, he had no edema, lymphadenopathy, abdominal tenderness, or skin rash. At the Level 1 hospital, the patient was treated for an unspecified gastrointestinal disorder with oral antipyretic medicine and electrolyte-fluid compensation. After 8 h, symptoms of pyrexia and diarrhea ceased.
At the 22nd hour, the first syncope was recorded and lasted for 40 s, accompanied by vomiting once. He was treated with intravenous (IV) transfusion with normal saline (0.9%) and closely monitored. At the 24th hour, he had the second syncope but no fever, vomiting, or convulsion. This syncope lasted for 35 s.
Due to the recurrent syncope, the patient was referred to our hospital at the 30th hour and admitted to the Emergency room. Symptoms and signs on admission were body temperature 36.5 C, blood pressure 105/65 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 bpm, oxygen saturation 93%, palpitation, fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea without vomiting. Glasgow Coma Scale was E4V5M6.   The abdomen was initially soft and mildly distended, with no significant bowel sounds and no tenderness with no visceromegaly or adenopathy. The third syncope occurred while the patient was in the Emergency room and lasted for 30 s, for which he was closely monitored without any treatment.
With three syncopes, mild dyspnea, electrocardiogram presented to change with sinus bradycardia, 40 bpm. IV atropine of 0.04 mg/kg of the body mass was prescribed. After the injection, the heart rate increased to 53 bpm (atropine test negative), suggesting a sickness sinus syndrome; therefore, he was planned to be treated with this diagnosis and indicated pace marker intervention (Figure 1).
On the other hand, due to pyrexia and digestive disorder symptoms, after being admitted to the emergency room, the patient was tested for S. typhi; the result was a Widal test positive, and the blood culture was positive for S. typhi.
Some medical tests were performed. The results of these tests were shown in Tables 1 and 2.
The patient was treated with oxygen support with a flow of 3 L/min x 120 min, saline 0.9% 500 mL IV, XXX drops/minute, atropine IV 0.04 mg/kg, and ciprofloxacin 500 mg oral x 2 tablets/day x 7 days.
After treatments, he was closely monitored on vital signs, oxygen saturation, and electrocardiogram for 7 days. No more syncope and no fever were recorded, and vital signs were normal. Heart rate increased day by day and remained stable from the sixth day (Figure 2).
Symptoms of headache, arthralgia, myalgia, and distended abdomen decreased and ceased on the sixth day. Electrocardiogram showed sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 72 bpm, and no sinus bradycardia was detected. The patient was discharged on the seventh day.
The patient was scheduled to get re-examinations on the 10th day, the first month, and the third month afterward. Results showed that no syncope, no pyrexia, and no digestive disorder symptoms occurred. Normal electrocardiographs with sinus rhythm and heart rate of 70-80 bpm were observed. The patient returns to normal life as usual.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presented with sudden-onset fever (39.2 °C), headache, arthralgia, myalgia, abdominal distension, and watery diarrhea, followed by three episodes of recurrent syncope over 30 hours.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented to a Level 1 hospital with sudden-onset pyrexia (39.2 °C), headache, arthralgia, myalgia, a distended abdomen, and four episodes of watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting. He was treated for an unspecified gastrointestinal disorder with oral antipyretics and fluid-electrolyte replacement, and his fever and diarrhea resolved after 8 hours. At the 22nd hour of illness, he experienced a first syncopal episode lasting 40 seconds accompanied by a single episode of vomiting, and received intravenous 0.9% normal saline. At the 24th hour, he had a second syncopal episode lasting 35 seconds without fever, vomiting, or convulsions. Due to recurrent syncope, he was referred to our Emergency Room at the 30th hour complaining of palpitations, fatigue, headache, dizziness, mild dyspnea, and nausea without vomiting.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously healthy with no prior history of typhoid vaccination.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, headache, dizziness, fatigue, palpitations, mild dyspnea, arthralgia, myalgia, abdominal distension, watery diarrhea, nausea, single episode of vomiting, and recurrent syncope. Pertinent negatives: no convulsions, skin rash, or edema.

objective.physical_examination: At the Level 1 hospital, temperature was 39.2 °C, blood pressure was 120/65 mmHg, and heart rate was 72 bpm, with no edema, lymphadenopathy, abdominal tenderness, or skin rash. On admission to our Emergency Room at the 30th hour, body temperature was 36.5 °C, blood pressure was 105/65 mmHg, respiratory rate was 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 93%; Glasgow Coma Scale score was E4V5M6 (15/15). The abdomen was soft and mildly distended with no significant bowel sounds, tenderness, visceromegaly, or adenopathy. A third syncopal episode lasting 30 seconds occurred in the Emergency Room.
objective.routine_investigations: Electrocardiogram (ECG) demonstrated sinus bradycardia at 40 bpm; following an intravenous atropine test (0.04 mg/kg), heart rate increased only to 53 bpm (negative atropine test, initially raising suspicion for sick sinus syndrome). Widal test was positive.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Typhoid fever complicated by severe sinus bradycardia and recurrent syncope, confirmed by blood culture positive for Salmonella typhi and positive Widal serology. Initial consideration of primary sick sinus syndrome requiring pacemaker implantation was superseded once S. typhi infection was confirmed. The patient was treated with supplemental oxygen (3 L/min for 120 minutes), intravenous 0.9% normal saline (500 mL), intravenous atropine (0.04 mg/kg), and oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days. Under close monitoring of vital signs, SpO2, and serial ECGs, no further syncope or fever occurred; his heart rate progressively increased and stabilized by day 6 (sinus rhythm at 72 bpm), and headache, arthralgia, myalgia, and abdominal distension resolved by day 6. He was discharged on day 7 and remained asymptomatic in normal sinus rhythm (70-80 bpm) at 10-day, 1-month, and 3-month follow-up visits.
